name: Envy
history: Raised by New Zealand's HortResearch from the same Braeburn x Royal Gala parentage as Jazz, and patented in 2008-09 as cultivar Scilate. Sold under the Envy trademark, it is grown under licence in New Zealand, Washington State, Chile, Australia and elsewhere.

look.description: Almost entirely bright red with yellow freckling showing through; the skin is notably thick and tough.

taste.summary: Very sweet with low acidity and a faint floral note; crisp, juicy, pale flesh that browns very slowly once cut. Firmness holds well in storage.

tree.notes: Licensed club variety; little published growing information outside commercial programmes.

pollination.notes: Needs a cross-pollinator; UK flowering group not published.

climate.best_climates: Long, sunny seasons with cool autumn nights, as in Hawke's Bay, central Washington and central Chile.
climate.poor_climates: Short, cool seasons where a late-October apple will not ripen fully; humid areas with high canker pressure.

health.other: Susceptible to European canker (Neonectria), sometimes carried without visible symptoms; growers have reported russet, shrivel, bitter pit and internal browning.

grow_notes: A late, long-season apple best left to warm, sunny commercial regions. If grown, choose a free-draining site to reduce canker risk and keep calcium levels up to limit bitter pit.

name: Ambrosia

origin.parentage: Chance seedling found among Jonagold trees; parents unknown, probably Golden Delicious with Starking (Red) Delicious or Jonagold

history: A chance seedling that came up in the Mennell family's orchard at Cawston in British Columbia's Similkameen Valley in the late 1980s, growing in a block of Jonagold. Its looks and sweetness led to commercial propagation in the 1990s, and it is now grown in Canada, Washington, New York, Chile, New Zealand and Europe.

look.description: Large, slightly conical fruit with a bright pinkish-red flush over a cream to pale yellow background.

taste.summary: Very sweet with almost no acidity, giving a pleasant but one-dimensional flavour with a pear-like note and, to some tasters, a light floral scent. Crisp and juicy though not as hard as Braeburn; left at room temperature it softens and turns more pear-like, and the cream flesh is slow to brown.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Jan; keep refrigerated, softens at room temperature

tree.notes: Comes into bearing young and crops regularly. Fruit ripens unevenly, so commercial orchards usually pick it in two passes.

pollination.notes: Listed in flowering group 4; needs a compatible diploid pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Sunny interior valleys with hot days and cold nights, like its home in southern British Columbia, central Washington and Ontario.
climate.poor_climates: Areas with heavy cedar-apple rust pressure in eastern North America unless sprayed; irrigation stress in hot dry orchards leads to soft scald and poor keeping.

health.other: Very susceptible to cedar-apple rust; some resistance to powdery mildew. Soft scald in store has been linked to water stress in the orchard.

grow_notes: Grow in full sun with steady irrigation in dry regions. Where junipers are nearby in North America, plan to control cedar-apple rust. Pick over two passes as fruit colours and ripens.

name: Cameo

origin.parentage: Chance seedling in a Red Delicious orchard; thought to be Red Delicious x Golden Delicious

history: Found in 1987 as a chance seedling in a Red Delicious block owned by the Caudle family near Dryden, Washington. It was propagated commercially in the 1990s and became one of Washington's more widely grown varieties.

look.description: Large fruit with bold red stripes and patches over a cream to orange-yellow ground, dotted with pale lenticels.

taste.summary: Dense, crisp and juicy, balancing sweetness with light tartness and a hint of pear. Orange Pippin's own note calls the flavour fairly bland, but many growers disagree, and individual tasters report strawberry or fresh-pineapple notes. It sweetens over a week or two of storage, browns slowly when cut and keeps its crunch for months in the fridge.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Feb; better after 1-2 weeks in store

pollination.notes: Listed in flowering group 3; needs a compatible diploid pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Dry, sunny irrigated fruit regions with cool autumn nights, like central Washington.
climate.poor_climates: Humid eastern North America where cedar-apple rust is rife; cool, short seasons may not ripen it fully.

health.other: Highly susceptible to cedar-apple rust; other disease ratings not well documented.

grow_notes: Best suited to sunny, dry regions. Control cedar-apple rust where junipers grow nearby, and store the crop for a couple of weeks before eating for best sweetness.

name: Pinova

origin.parentage: Clivia (Geheimrat Dr. Oldenburg x Cox's Orange Pippin) x Golden Delicious

history: Bred at the fruit research institute at Dresden-Pillnitz in what was then East Germany from a 1965 cross, and released in 1986. It is grown across Europe and sold in the USA as Piñata and in France as Corail.

look.description: Golden Delicious shape with orange-red stripes and flush over a yellow ground.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy and fairly tender, with an intense sweet flavour balanced by enough tartness; several tasters notice a floral scent reminiscent of roses. It shows its Cox ancestry and keeps three months or more without losing quality.

tree.notes: Rather weak-growing spur-bearer that crops heavily and regularly; suits small trees and intensive systems.

pollination.notes: Listed in flowering group 4. Sources disagree on its value as a pollen donor (one rates it poor, another good), so add a reliable pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Temperate central and western Europe, including mild damp climates, and sunny fruit regions with warm rather than hot summers; blossom has some frost resistance.
climate.poor_climates: Very hot summers are likely to reduce colour and storage quality; short-season northern sites may not ripen it.

health.other: Generally good disease resistance with some resistance to scab and canker; somewhat susceptible to powdery mildew.

grow_notes: A reliable, compact garden apple for warmer parts of the UK. Thin heavy crops for size, keep mildew in check in spring, and plant with a group 3-5 pollinator.

name: SweeTango

origin.raised_by: University of Minnesota (David Bedford, James Luby)

history: Bred at the University of Minnesota from a 1988 Honeycrisp x Zestar! cross and patented in 2008 as cultivar Minneiska. It is sold as SweeTango and grown under a managed licence by a growers' cooperative in the northern USA and Canada.

look.description: Medium to large fruit with a red flush and streaks over yellow-green.

taste.summary: Explosively crunchy and juicy in the Honeycrisp mould but with a livelier sweet-tart balance; tasters describe floral, lightly spicy notes (one found a trace of cinnamon) and citrus hints have also been reported. Best eaten soon after harvest: fruit left at room temperature turns mealy and bland within a week or two, and it does not bake well.

tree.notes: Bears young. A managed variety, so trees are mostly restricted to licensed growers.

pollination.notes: Needs a cross-pollinator; UK flowering group not published.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter northern regions with cool summer nights: Minnesota, Michigan, New York, Quebec, Nova Scotia and similar.
climate.poor_climates: Hot-summer, mild-winter areas where its Honeycrisp heritage suggests soft, poorly coloured fruit.

grow_notes: Bred for cold northern orchards. Pick as soon as ripe and eat within a few weeks, as it does not keep its best texture for long.

name: Ariane
history: A scab-resistant apple from INRA's breeding programme at Angers, built over several generations from lines carrying the Vf resistance gene (originally from Malus floribunda) and selected from a (Florina x Prima) x Golden Delicious cross. It was introduced around 2000, with the first commercial orchards in 2002, and is grown in France for low-spray production.

look.description: Smallish fruit with a bright crimson flush over golden-green and a noticeably indented base.

taste.summary: Very crisp, dense, firm cream flesh that is moist rather than truly juicy, with a balanced sweet-sharp taste, a hint of pear-drop and a delicate fragrance; best eaten slightly chilled. Orange Pippin advises eating it within about a week rather than keeping it, which sits oddly with its reputation as a late keeper.

tree.notes: Vigorous, spur-bearing tree prone to alternate cropping; needs careful pruning in the first years so light reaches the fruit for colour.

pollination.notes: Early-to-mid flowering over a long period (listed in group 2). Santana, Gala and GoldRush have been suggested as partners.

climate.best_climates: Temperate western Europe, especially the Loire and other French fruit regions; useful anywhere scab pressure is high.
climate.poor_climates: Shady or dull sites where the crimson colour fails to develop; very hot regions are untested.

health.other: Carries Vf (and reportedly Vg) scab resistance, effective against common scab races though Vf-breaking strains exist; reported to cope reasonably with other diseases.

grow_notes: A good low-spray choice for wet climates. Thin firmly to curb biennial bearing and keep the canopy open so fruit colours; pair with a group 2-3 diploid.
